claim: Salivary fluid secretion involves an intricate choreography of membrane transporters to result in the trans-epithelial movement of NaCl and water into the acinus lumen.
source: Salivary fluid secretion involves an intricate choreography of membrane transporters to result in the trans-epithelial movement of NaCl and water into the acinus lumen.
evidence: This is a general statement about salivary secretion that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Current models of salivary secretion are largely based on experimental observations in enzymatically isolated cells where the Ca2+ signal invariably propagates globally.
source: Current models are largely based on experimental observations in enzymatically isolated cells where the Ca2+ signal invariably propagates globally and thus appears ideally suited to activate spatially separated Cl and K channels, present on the apical and basolateral plasma membrane, respectively.
evidence: This statement references prior experimental work and models in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Ca2+ signals were initiated in the apical endoplasmic reticulum following nerve stimulation in live mice.
source: Consistent with in vitro studies, Ca2+ signals were initiated in the apical endoplasmic reticulum.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations described in the Results section.

claim: Highly localized trains of Ca2+ transients that failed to fully propagate from the apical region were observed in vivo, in marked contrast to in vitro data.
source: In marked contrast to in vitro data, highly localized trains of Ca2+ transients that failed to fully propagate from the apical region were observed.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by imaging data presented in Figures 8-10.

claim: Large apical-basal Ca2+ gradients were elicited following stimuli optimum for secretion.
source: Following stimuli optimum for secretion, large apical-basal gradients were elicited.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 9 and 10.

claim: Salivary fluid secretion is vital to the health of the oral cavity.
source: Salivary fluid secretion is vital to the health of the oral cavity (Pedersen et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pedersen et al., 2002.

claim: Patients with salivary hypofunction experience difficulty chewing and swallowing food, speaking and are susceptible to oral infections that result in dental caries.
source: This is most clearly appreciated in disease states which result in hypofunction where patients experience difficulty chewing and swallowing food, speaking and are susceptible to oral infections that result in dental caries (Melvin, 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Melvin, 1991.

claim: Fluid secretion from the salivary gland requires the trans epithelial movement of Cl- across polarized acinar cells.
source: Fluid secretion from the salivary gland requires the trans epithelial movement of Cl- across polarized acinar cells (Foskett, 1990; Melvin, 1999; Melvin et al., 2005; Turner and Sugiya, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cl- enters the lumen of the acinus across the apical PM through TMEM16a chloride channels.
source: and subsequently enters the lumen of the acinus across the apical PM through TMEM16a chloride channels (Romanenko et al., 2010a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Romanenko et al., 2010a.

claim: An elevation in cytosolic [Ca2+] following neurotransmitter release plays a central role in the stimulation of fluid secretion from salivary gland acinar cells.
source: An elevation in cytosolic [Ca2+] following neurotransmitter release plays a central role in the stimulation of fluid secretion from salivary gland acinar cells (Ambudkar, 2011; Ambudkar, 2016; Gallacher and Petersen, 1983; Putney, 1982; Weiss et al., 1982).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Acetylcholine (ACh) is the primary neurotransmitter released following parasympathetic input to the major salivary glands after gustatory and olfactory stimulation.
source: Acetylcholine (ACh) is the primary neurotransmitter released following parasympathetic input to the major salivary glands after gustatory and olfactory stimulation (Matsui et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Matsui et al., 2000.

claim: ACh results in activation of muscarinic receptors, G-protein coupled stimulation of inositol 1,4,5 trisphosphate (IP3) production and subsequent Ca2+ release from endoplasmic reticulum stores via IP3 receptors (IP3R).
source: ACh results in activation of muscarinic receptors, G-protein coupled stimulation of inositol 1,4,5 trisphosphate (IP3) production and subsequent Ca2+ release from endoplasmic reticulum stores via IP3 receptors (IP3R) (Futatsugi et al., 2005; Lee et al., 1997; Pages et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: ER stores are subsequently refilled by store operated Ca2+ entry across the PM, which is required for sustained salivary secretion.
source: The ER stores are subsequently refilled by store operated Ca2+ entry across the PM, which is required for sustained salivary secretion (Cheng et al., 2011a; Cheng et al., 2011b; Melvin et al., 1991; Takemura et al., 1989).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The primary effector of the increase in [Ca2+] to stimulate saliva flow are TMEM16a channels localized in the apical PM.
source: To stimulate saliva flow, the primary effector of the increase in [Ca2+] are TMEM16a channels localized in the apical PM (Romanenko et al., 2010a; Arreola et al., 1996a; Arreola et al., 1996b; Begenisich and Melvin, 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Ca2+ increases the activity of K channels, conventionally thought to be localized predominantly at the basolateral PM, to maintain the membrane potential to favor continued Cl- exit and secretion.
source: As Cl- moves across the apical PM, the membrane potential approaches the equilibrium potential for Cl-; however, Ca2+ also increases the activity of K channels, conventionally thought to be localized predominantly at the basolateral PM, to maintain the membrane potential to favor continued Cl- exit and secretion (Maruyama et al., 1983; Nakamoto et al., 2008; Nakamoto et al., 2007; Romanenko et al., 2007; Romanenko et al., 2010b).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In isolated salivary gland acinar cells, agonist-stimulated Ca2+ signals are initiated in the extreme apical ER followed by a rapid Ca2+ wave which results in globalization of the signal throughout the cytoplasm.
source: For example, stimulation with muscarinic agonists, or more directly by photolysis of caged-IP3, invariably results in the Ca2+ signal initiating in the extreme apical ER followed by a rapid Ca2+ wave which results in globalization of the signal throughout the cytoplasm (Bruce et al., 2004; Bruce et al., 2002; Giovannucci et al., 2002; Larina and Thorn, 2005; Tojyo et al., 1997; Won et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations describing in vitro studies.

claim: The initiation sites of Ca2+ signals, termed the 'trigger zone', correspond to the localization of the majority of type-2/3 IP3R.
source: The initiation sites, termed the 'trigger zone', correspond to the localization of the majority of type-2/3 IP3R (Lee et al., 1997; Pages et al., 2019)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lee et al., 1997 and Pages et al., 2019.

claim: The distance between apical ER and PM is estimated to be ~50–100 nm.
source: Super-resolution STED imaging does resolve distinct distributions of the two proteins, such that the distance between apical ER and PM is estimated to be ~50–100 nm (Sneyd et al., 2021)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sneyd et al., 2021.

claim: At low agonist concentrations in vitro, the Ca2+ signal is manifested as a series of oscillations with a relatively slow period (5–8/min).
source: At low agonist concentrations, the cycle of apical Ca2+ release, global spread and subsequent Ca2+ sequestration is repeated, such that temporally, the Ca2+ signal is manifested as a series of oscillations with a relatively slow period (5–8/min) (Bruce et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bruce et al., 2002.

claim: Transgenic mice expressing GCaMP6f specifically in exocrine acinar cells were generated by crossing homozygous GCaMP6f mice with heterozygous tamoxifen-inducible Mist1 Cre mice.
source: To generate mice expressing a fluorescent Ca2+ indicator in exocrine acinar cells, homozygous mice expressing the fast genetically encoded Ca2+ indicator GCaMP6f (B6J.Cg-Gt(ROSA)26Sortm95.1(CAG-GCaMP6f)Hze/MwarJ) (Chen et al., 2013) floxed by a STOP cassette, were crossed with heterozygous tamoxifen-inducible Mist1 Cre mice (B6.129-Bhlha15tm3(cre/ERT2)Skz/J) (Maruyama et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used to generate the transgenic mice, with citations to the mouse strains.

claim: GCaMP6f expression was uniformly observed in essentially all acinar cells while GCaMP6f expression was not evident in any other cell type such as blood vessels, nerves, myoepithelial cells or ductal cells.
source: GCaMP6f expression was uniformly observed in essentially all acinar cells while GCaMP6f expression was not evident in any other cell type such as blood vessels, nerves, myoepithelial cells or ductal cells.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Electrical stimulation at various stimulus strengths (1–100 Hz, 12 s) delivered to nerves innervating the SMG induced increases in intracellular [Ca2+] in acinar cells.
source: Electrical stimulation at various stimulus strengths delivered to nerves innervating the SMG (1–100 Hz, 12 s initiated at 10 s) induced increases in intracellular [Ca2+] in acinar cells (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Following 1 Hz stimulation, a minority of the cells exhibited small, rapid changes in fluorescence, while most cells were refractory.
source: Following 1 Hz stimulation, a minority of the cells exhibited small, rapid changes in fluorescence, (n = 4 fields from four animals, Figure 2A,B), while most cells were refractory.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Following higher frequency stimulation (3–10 Hz), the majority of the cells in the field responded and the amplitude of the [Ca2+] signal increased as the stimulation strength was increased.
source: Following higher frequency stimulation (3–10 Hz), the majority of the cells in the field responded and the amplitude of the [Ca2+] signal increased as the stimulation strength was increased (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The contralateral SMG were unresponsive to even the highest 100 Hz nerve bundle stimulation of the ipsilateral gland.
source: Of note, the stimulation likely led to increased neural activity specifically, rather than stimulating acinar cells directly, as a consequence of current leak through the saline depolarizing nerve endings, as the contralateral SMG were unresponsive to even the highest 100 Hz nerve bundle stimulation of the ipsilateral gland (p > 0.1 compared to without stimulation, n=4 fields from four animals, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There was no significant secretion activated by 1–3 Hz nerve stimulation for 1 min.
source: There was no significant secretion activated by 1–3 Hz nerve stimulation for 1 min (p > 0.05 compared to the absence of nerve stimulation, n = four animals)
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Saliva secretion progressively increased following 5–10 Hz nerve stimulation.
source: but saliva secretion progressively increased following 5–10 Hz nerve stimulation (p < 0.05 compared to the absence of stimulation, n = four animals) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At moderate stimulation intensity (0–10 Hz), there was a linear correlation between the peak [Ca2+] increases by stimulation and saliva secretion (r2 = 0.995).
source: At moderate stimulation intensity (0–10 Hz), there was a linear correlation between the peak [Ca2+] increases by stimulation and saliva secretion (r2 = 0.995, n = four animals, Figure 3B).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Sustained saliva secretion requires both Ca2+ release and subsequent Ca2+ influx.
source: Sustained saliva secretion requires both Ca2+ release and subsequent Ca2+ influx (Ambudkar, 2011; Cheng et al., 2011b; Ambudkar et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The Orai channel blocker GSK7975A significantly attenuated the plateau Ca2+ response measured following 5 min of 10 Hz stimulation.
source: However, the plateau measured following 5 min of stimulation was significantly attenuated in drug injected animals vs. vehicle (Figure 4A, pooled data in Figure 4B/C) suggesting a requirement for Orai channel dependent influx for sustained Ca2+ signals and secretion.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: GSK7975A had no significant effect on the magnitude of the initial peak Ca2+ response to 10 Hz stimulation.
source: No significant effect was observed on the magnitude of the initial peak, presumably because sufficient refilling of the ER Ca2+ store had occurred during exposure to blocker.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: At 1 Hz stimulation, 34.0 ± 5.1% of the sub-regions showed significant responses during the stimulation.
source: Overall, 34.0 ± 5.1% (n = 19 fields from eight animals) of the sub-regions showed significant responses during the stimulation (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: At 1 Hz stimulation, the increase in [Ca2+] in the responding regions exhibited a prolonged latency prior to the initial rise following stimulation (6.72 ± 0.79 s).
source: Moreover, the increase in [Ca2+] in the responding regions exhibited a prolonged latency prior to the initial rise following stimulation (6.72 ± 0.79 s, n = 19, Figure 5H).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: At 10 Hz, virtually all regions responded to the stimulation (98.5 ± 0.6%) with minimal latency (1.70 ± 0.27 s).
source: At 10 Hz, virtually all regions responded to the stimulation (98.5 ± 0.6%, n = 19) with minimal latency (1.70 ± 0.27 s, n = 19) (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 5G,H.

claim: The amplitude of the maximal increase in [Ca2+] in the subdivided grids increased as the strength of the stimulation was augmented.
source: Further, the amplitude of the maximal increase in [Ca2+] in the subdivided grids also increased as the strength of the stimulation was augmented (Figure 5I)
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Grids which responded at lower stimulus intensity also strongly responded to higher frequency stimulation.
source: This analysis demonstrated a clear pattern whereby, at each stimulus strength, particular regions of the field of view were most susceptible to stimulation, such that grids giving the largest amplitude response at 1 Hz similarly responded by displaying the largest amplitude signals at 3, 5 and 10 Hz stimulation. (n = 5 fields from four animals) (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: High-responding grid regions showed linearly enhanced increases following stimulation (R2 = 0.9197).
source: High-responding grid regions showed linearly enhanced increases following stimulation (R2 = 0.9197, n = 4 fields from four animals), while the increase in Ca2+ signal following increased stimulation in less responsive regions was proportionately smaller (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Physostigmine enhanced the peak amplitude of the Ca2+ signals following stimulation.
source: Physostigmine (0.1 mg/kg body weight IP) enhanced the peak amplitude of the Ca2+ signals following stimulation (Figure 7A–D)
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 7A-D.

claim: The augmentation in the Ca2+ signal by physostigmine was not statistically significant at 1 Hz stimulation.
source: The augmentation in the Ca2+ signal was not statistically significant at 1 Hz stimulation (p > 0.05, n = 5 fields from four animals)
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 7E-G.

claim: Physostigmine augmentation became more prominent at 3 Hz with shorter latency, an increase in the number of responding grids and peak amplitude.
source: but became more prominent at 3 Hz with shorter latency, an increase in the number of responding grids and peak amplitude (p < 0.05 in % response and peak ΔF/F, n = 5)
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 7E-G.

claim: At all physiological stimulus strengths the increase in [Ca2+]i was highly heterogeneous, with the largest increases in signal occurring in the apical aspects of acinar clusters, directly below the apical PM.
source: This analysis revealed that at all physiological stimulus strengths the increase in [Ca2+]i was highly heterogeneous, with the largest increases in signal occurring in the apical aspects of acinar clusters, directly below the apical PM (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: At 5 Hz stimulation, the signal consisted of brief (< 2 s in duration), repetitive increases in [Ca2+] that were highly localized, being initiated in, and almost entirely confined to the apical portions of individual cells, within a few μms of the apical PM.
source: In marked contrast to in vitro experiments, analysis of the image series demonstrated that the signal consisted of brief (< 2 s in duration), repetitive increases in [Ca2+] (Figure 8B). The signals were highly localized, being initiated in, and almost entirely confined to the apical portions of individual cells, within a few μms of the apical PM (Figure 8B–E)
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 8B-E.

claim: At 10 Hz stimulation, a rise in [Ca2+] was rapidly initiated in the extreme apical ER, close to the apical PM, and Ca2+ signals were observed in the basal aspects of the cell but of considerably lower amplitude, approximately 20–30% of that observed in the apical domain.
source: At 10 Hz stimulation, a rise in [Ca2+] was also rapidly initiated in the extreme apical ER, close to the apical PM (imaging field in Figure 9A with red box showing the highlighted cluster depicted in Figure 9B). In contrast to lower stimulus strengths, Ca2+ signals were observed in the basal aspects of the cell (Figure 9B–E), but of considerably lower amplitude, approximately 20–30% of that observed in the apical domain.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Line scan analysis demonstrated that at each stimulus intensity the signal rapidly decays away from the apical initiation sites to the nucleus and is ~25% of the apical signal in the extreme base of the cell.
source: The apical-basal gradient was further analyzed by plotting the amplitude of the maximum fluorescent change across the line profile which further reinforces that at each stimulus intensity the signal rapidly decays away from the apical initiation sites to the nucleus and is ~25% of the apical signal in the extreme base of the cell (Figure 10. BIII, CIII and DIII).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 10.

claim: The frequency of Ca2+ oscillations was markedly faster (~1 Hz) when measured in vivo than previously described in isolated cells (~0.2 Hz).
source: This demonstrated that the frequency of oscillations was markedly faster (~1 Hz) when measured in vivo than previously described in isolated cells (~0.2 Hz, this study, Figure 12)
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 11 and Figure 12.

claim: The frequency of oscillations modestly increased between 3 and 5 Hz stimulation.
source: and further modestly increased between 3 and 5 Hz stimulation (Figure 11E; 79 ROIs experiment shown in Figure 11A–C and pooled data from 13 individual fields from five animals (Figure 11F)).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 11E,F.

claim: The relationship between secretion and the frequency of Ca2+ oscillation was less strong (R2 = 0.824) than the correlation between saliva secretion and the magnitude of the evoked Ca2+ signal.
source: In contrast to the robust correlation between saliva secretion and the magnitude of the evoked Ca2+ signal, the relationship between secretion and the frequency of Ca2+ oscillation was less strong (R2 = 0.824, Figure 11G).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 11G.

claim: In acutely isolated GCaMP6f expressing acini, individual acinar cells failed to respond to 5 nM CCh; however, at 25 nM CCh single cells within an acinus responded by evoking repetitive Ca2+ transients with a frequency ~0.2 Hz.
source: Individual acinar cells failed to respond to 5 nM CCh; however, at 25 nM CCh single cells within an acinus responded by evoking repetitive Ca2+ transients (Figure 12) with a frequency ~0.2 Hz.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 12.

claim: Oscillations evoked even by threshold concentrations of CCh were initiated below the apical PM and invariably globalized with all CCh concentrations.
source: Oscillations evoked even by threshold concentrations of CCh were initiated below the apical PM and invariably globalized with all CCh concentrations (Figure 12D–F and Video 5).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 12D-F and Video 5.

claim: The spatiotemporal profile of the Ca2+ responses evoked in acutely isolated GCaMP6f expressing acini were strikingly similar to numerous reports documenting agonist-evoked Ca2+ responses with conventional chemical Ca2+ indicators.
source: In total, the spatiotemporal profile of the Ca2+ responses evoked in acutely isolated GCaMP6f expressing acini were strikingly similar to numerous reports documenting agonist-evoked Ca2+ responses with conventional chemical Ca2+ indicators and thus the properties of the genetically encoded indicator at physiological temperature per se do not explain the differences observed.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the current in vitro data with previous literature.

claim: A new mathematical model incorporating apical KCa channels and localized Ca2+ signals was constructed.
source: A new mathematical model, incorporating these data was constructed to probe how salivary secretion can be optimally stimulated by apical Ca2+ signals.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and described in detail in the Results and Methods sections.

claim: In the new model, the apical region includes all the components necessary for saliva secretion, with KCa channels and Na/K ATPases in addition to the TMEM16a channels.
source: The apical region is defined as the domain within 3 μm of the apical PM, which is itself demarcated by the tight junctions. This region now includes all the components necessary for saliva secretion, with KCa channels and Na/K ATPases in addition to the TMEM16a channels (Figure 13)
evidence: This is directly stated and illustrated in Figure 13.

claim: Model simulations show that as VPLC increases, the [Ca2+] oscillation frequency increases and the latency decreases.
source: As VPLC increases, the [Ca2+] oscillation frequency increases and the latency decreases.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by model simulations shown in Figure 14A.

claim: Model simulations show that absence of both a propagated [Ca2+] wave and apical KCa channels significantly decreases saliva secretion.
source: These simulations show that absence of both a propagated [Ca2+] wave and apical KCa channels significantly decreases saliva secretion.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by model simulations shown in Figure 14B.

claim: In the new model, basal [Ca2+] is between 25% and 35% of apical [Ca2+], as observed experimentally.
source: In the new model (Figure 14C), basal [Ca2+] is between 25% and 35% of apical [Ca2+], as observed experimentally
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by model simulations shown in Figure 14C.

claim: Model simulations show that optimal fluid secretion occurs when the apical and basal KCa densities are approximately equal.
source: Optimal fluid secretion occurs when the apical and basal KCa densities are approximately equal.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by model simulations shown in Figure 14F.

claim: KCa3.1 and KCa1.1 together with Na/K ATPases are present in the apical PM of salivary acinar cells.
source: Previously, however we have demonstrated, both functionally and physically, that the KCa channels, KCa3.1 ('IK') and KCa1.1 ('BK') together with Na/K ATPases are present in the apical PM of salivary acinar cells (Almássy et al., 2018; Almassy et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: KCa3.1 colocalized with apical markers including IP3R3 and Zona occludens-1.
source: Notably, we reported that KCa3.1 colocalized with apical markers including IP3R3 and Zona occludens-1.
evidence: This statement refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: Focal, highly localized uncaging of Ca2+, directly below the apical PM resulted in activation of a K+ conductance with pharmacology consistent with KCa3.1.
source: Further, focal, highly localized uncaging of Ca2+, directly below the apical PM resulted in activation of a K+ conductance with pharmacology consistent with KCa3.1.
evidence: This statement refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: Apical uncaging of Ca2+ evoked a smaller current in acini prepared from KCa1.1 knockout transgenic mice.
source: Additionally, apical uncaging of Ca2+ evoked a smaller current in acini prepared from KCa1.1 knockout transgenic mice (Almassy et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Local, non-propagating Ca2+ signals are observed in isolated pancreatic acinar cell in response to IP3, low concentrations of secretagogues and physiological concentrations of the gut hormone cholecystokinin.
source: Local, non-propagating Ca2+ signals are observed in isolated pancreatic acinar cell in response to IP3, low concentrations of secretagogues and physiological concentrations of the gut hormone cholecystokinin (Ashby et al., 2003; Thorn et al., 1993; Thorn et al., 1996; Thorn and Petersen, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The failure of the signal to propagate and standing [Ca2+] gradients observed are presumably established by SERCA, PMCA and mitochondrial buffering to efficiently reduce the local [Ca2+] to levels that do not support substantial CICR through IP3R and RYR.
source: The failure of the signal to propagate and standing [Ca2+] gradients observed are presumably established by SERCA, PMCA and mitochondrial buffering to efficiently reduce the local [Ca2+] to levels that do not support substantial CICR through IP3R and RYR that are presumed to be localized in the ER distant from the apical trigger zone.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation proposed by the authors based on their observations.

claim: The complex architecture of the SMG lobule is maintained by junctional complexes and interactions with the extracellular matrix and stromal cells.
source: At the level of the SMG lobule, the polarity of individual cells and their organization within an acinus is vital for function. The complex architecture is maintained by junctional complexes and interactions with the extracellular matrix and stromal cells (Baker, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Baker, 2010.

claim: Enzymic digestion may disrupt the exquisite polarity of acinar cells, leading to altered Ca2+ signaling characteristics.
source: Clearly, these interactions may be disturbed when cells are isolated from an excised gland by enzymic digestion. An apparent consequence may be a disruption of the exquisite polarity of acinar cells. Perturbed localization of the Ca2+ signaling machinery could disrupt the balance between Ca2+ release and clearance to ultimately result in an alteration of the spatiotemporal characteristics of the signal.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation proposed by the authors to explain differences between in vivo and in vitro observations.
